"Mohit, you asked how we got back on our feet after the flood. I, Harish, your old neighbour, will tell you straight: for the first month, we didn't.
I was twenty-one. The water took the ground floor, my certificates, the shop stock. I sat on the steps every day doing nothing but feeling heavy. Then one night I couldn't sleep and I thought, I'm waiting for everything to fix itself at once. It won't.
So I made stages on a sheet of paper. Week one: apply for the government relief at the ward office. Week two: the insurance claim, with the photos I'd luckily taken on my phone before cleaning. Week three: go to the college and the tehsil office to replace my lost papers, one by one.
And stage four, which I nearly skipped: talk to the counsellor at the relief camp. I thought that was for weak people. It wasn't. It was the stage that let me finish the others."

Stage three: new copies of the ration card and her marksheets, one office each week. Stage four: the counsellor who visited the camp on Thursdays.

I'm Binita, from the flat next door in Guwahati. Last Sunday I heard a lot of thumping and giggling through the wall, so I went over.
Chandrika had her two little brothers crouched under the heavy dining table. "Drop," she said, and they dropped. "Cover," and they tucked in, arms over their heads. "Hold on," and they grabbed the table legs.
She explained to them out loud, and I think partly to herself: "When the shaking starts, your legs want to run. But running is when things fall on you. So we practise until your body goes to the table without thinking."
Then she walked them to the door and the stairwell, pointing. "Not the lift. Never the lift."
They did it five times. By the fifth, the younger one was under the table before she'd finished saying "drop". I can't know what she was feeling, but she looked serious and satisfied.

qa.a: She chose the heavy dining table.

qa.q: What might Chandrika have been feeling during the drill?
qa.a: She seemed serious and satisfied, perhaps a little worried about a real quake but pleased that her brothers learned quickly.

qa.q: What else could Chandrika add to the family's preparation?
qa.a: She could practise the drill at night too, or in a different room, so the brothers know what to do wherever they are.

qa.q: How might Binita see the drill after watching?

Saturday. After the small tremor on Thursday, Shalini noticed what she and her little brother Asif had done: they had both run into the corridor. She sat down with a notebook. "Running felt right, but the corridor has the glass cabinet. What should we have done?"
She looked it up in the district disaster guide: get down low, get under something sturdy, and grip it until the shaking stops. Then she walked through the flat, looking for sturdy cover. The study desk, yes. The glass cabinet side, never. The exit: the stairs, not the lift.
Sunday. She practised with Asif. "Drop." He flopped on the floor. "Cover." He crawled under the desk. "Hold on." He grabbed the leg. They did it in his room, the kitchen and the living room.
The next Wednesday. Asif's school ran a surprise drill. That evening he announced, "I was first under the table. My teacher said well done." Shalini just smiled.

Dear Samir,
Thank you for all your calls last week. I can finally write properly.
When the water trapped us on the first floor, I panicked the first night. We ate dinner as usual, drank as much as we liked, and kept the lights on until the inverter died.
The next morning I realised we didn't know how long this would last. So I counted everything: nine litres of drinking water, a kilo of rice, bread, two packets of biscuits, some fruit. I divided it for two more days for four of us, with water first for Nani. No more cooking rice that wasted water.
Then relatives. Phones barely worked, so I sent short texts instead of calls, since those got through. I reached Mama in Silchar and asked him to check on Mami's family downstream. He did; they were safe.
The boat came on day three. We still had a litre left.
Bhavna

The first evening, we ate like it was normal. Then I looked at what we'd carried up: six bottles of water, a bag of flattened rice, some jaggery, a few bananas. And I thought, what if it's three days? Nobody knows.

Our phones were almost dead. Calls wouldn't go through, but texts sometimes did. So I switched off both phones and turned one on every three hours to send one message to my uncle and check for replies.
On day two the reply came: the rescue boat was coming."

passage:
The college counselling centre was quiet at four. Vaibhav sat across from the counsellor with his friend Leela beside him, which was the first step he'd planned.
"I've been going to this group for two months," he said. "Lately they want me at meetings alone with the leader. When I said I wanted to take a break, he said I'd 'regret betraying the family'."
The counsellor listened. "What are you thinking of doing?"
Vaibhav had written it down. "I've told Leela everything. I won't meet anyone from the group alone. I'll stop going from this week. I've told my parents; they're driving down on Saturday. And if anyone threatens me, I'll go to the police."
"That's a good plan," the counsellor said. "Let's add one thing: if anyone from the group turns up at the hostel, tell the warden straight away." The counsellor called the hostel warden while they were still in the room.
Leela squeezed his arm on the way out.

qa.q: Who did Vaibhav bring to the counselling centre?
qa.a: He brought his friend Leela.

qa.q: How was Vaibhav feeling about the leader's words?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and pressured, especially by private meetings and being told he would regret betraying the family.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav do to stay safe in the weeks after leaving?
qa.a: He could keep Leela and the warden informed of any contact from the group and save any threatening messages for the police.

qa.q: How does the plan look to the counsellor?
qa.a: The counsellor sees it as a good, careful plan and strengthens it by adding the warden and calling the warden at once.

grounding: Shows the person stepping away from a group with a trusted friend, no private meetings, family support and police if threatened, with the college acting too.

Himani,
I'm writing because you asked why I stopped going to the Sunday group. I didn't want to explain in the canteen.
It started feeling wrong in March. The leader began asking me to stay after sessions to talk alone. He said I was "special" and shouldn't tell my family about our talks. My stomach turned every time.
So I made a plan and didn't do it alone. First I told my friend Tenzin everything. Then I stopped meeting anyone from the group without someone else present. I called my parents; Papa came that weekend and stayed two days. I simply stopped going.
Two members kept messaging, saying I'd "regret leaving". When one wrote that they knew where my hostel was, Papa and I went to the police station and showed them the messages. The officer noted it and called the member. The messages stopped.
If you ever feel that twist in your stomach there, tell me.
Leela

qa.q: Who did Leela tell first about the group?
qa.a: Leela told her friend Tenzin everything first.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the leader asked for private talks?
qa.a: Leela felt uneasy and frightened, with a stomach that turned every time.

qa.q: What else could Himani do if she starts feeling uneasy in the group?
qa.a: Himani could tell Leela or a family member, avoid being alone with leaders, and step away with someone's support.

qa.q: How might Leela's father have felt when he saw the messages?
qa.a: Papa likely felt protective and worried, which is why he went with Leela to the police station.

grounding: Shows the person, feeling uneasy, telling a trusted friend, avoiding private meetings with the leader, stopping attending and going to the police when threatened.
